    98→
    99→def generate_env_from_config(config_path: Path, base_env_path: Path, output_dir: Path = None) -> Path:
   100→    """
   101→    Generate an .env file from an experiment configuration.
   102→
   103→    Args:
   104→        config_path: Path to the experiment config YAML
   105→        base_env_path: Path to the base .env file to copy from
   106→        output_dir: Directory to save the generated .env file (default: same as config)
   107→
   108→    Returns:
   109→        Path to the generated .env file
   110→    """
   111→    # Load base env and config
   112→    env_content = load_base_env(base_env_path)
   113→    config = load_experiment_config(config_path)
   114→
   115→    # Extract LLM settings from config
   116→    llm_config = config.get('llm', {})
   117→    env_settings = config.get('env_settings', {})
   118→
   119→    provider = llm_config.get('provider', env_settings.get('LLM_SERVICE_PROVIDER', 'openai'))
   120→    model = llm_config.get('model', env_settings.get('LLM_SERVICE_MODEL', 'gpt-4o'))
   121→    temperature = llm_config.get('temperature', env_settings.get('LLM_TEMPERATURE', 0.0))
   122→
   123→    # Update env content with new values
   124→    env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'LLM_SERVICE_PROVIDER', provider)
   125→    env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'LLM_SERVICE_MODEL', model)
   126→    env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'LLM_TEMPERATURE', str(temperature))
   127→
   128→    # Set the import path based on provider
   129→    import_path = get_provider_import_path(provider)
   130→    env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'LLM_PROVIDER_IMPORT_PATH', import_path)
   131→
   132→    # Set the service token based on provider
   133→    api_key = get_api_key_for_provider(provider, env_content)
   134→    if api_key:
   135→        env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'LLM_SERVICE_TOKEN', api_key)
   136→
   137→    # Handle base_url and context_length for Ollama
   138→    if 'ollama' in provider.lower():
   139→        base_url = llm_config.get('base_url', 'http://localhost:11434')
   140→        env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'LLM_BASE_URL', base_url)
   141→
   142→        context_length = llm_config.get('context_length')
   143→        if context_length is not None:
   144→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH', str(context_length))
   145→
   146→    # Handle prompts configuration
   147→    prompts_config = config.get('prompts', {})
   148→    if prompts_config:
   149→        base_dir = prompts_config.get('prompts_base_dir', '')
   150→        # Resolve relative to config file location
   151→        if base_dir and not os.path.isabs(base_dir):
   152→            base_dir = str((config_path.parent / base_dir).resolve())
   153→
   154→        system_dir = prompts_config.get('system_prompt_dir', '')
   155→        if system_dir:
   156→            full_system_dir = str(Path(base_dir) / system_dir) if base_dir else str((config_path.parent / system_dir).resolve())
   157→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'HARMONIA_PROMPTS_DIR', full_system_dir)
   158→
   159→        react_prelude = prompts_config.get('react_prelude', '')
   160→        if react_prelude:
   161→            full_react = str(Path(base_dir) / react_prelude) if base_dir else str((config_path.parent / react_prelude).resolve())
   162→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'HARMONIA_REACT_PRELUDE', full_react)
   163→
   164→        code_context_prompt = prompts_config.get('code_context_prompt', '')
   165→        if code_context_prompt:
   166→            full_code = str(Path(base_dir) / code_context_prompt) if base_dir else str((config_path.parent / code_context_prompt).resolve())
   167→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'HARMONIA_CODE_CONTEXT_PROMPT', full_code)
   168→
   169→        codeact_prompt = prompts_config.get('codeact_prompt', '')
   170→        if codeact_prompt:
   171→            full_codeact = str(Path(base_dir) / codeact_prompt) if base_dir else str((config_path.parent / codeact_prompt).resolve())
   172→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'HARMONIA_CODEACT_PROMPT', full_codeact)
   173→
   174→        codeact_summary_template = prompts_config.get('codeact_summary_template', '')
   175→        if codeact_summary_template:
   176→            full_summary = str(Path(base_dir) / codeact_summary_template) if base_dir else str((config_path.parent / codeact_summary_template).resolve())
   177→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'HARMONIA_CODEACT_SUMMARY_TEMPLATE', full_summary)
   178→
   179→        tool_prompts_dir = prompts_config.get('tool_prompts_dir', '')
   180→        if tool_prompts_dir:
   181→            full_tools = str(Path(base_dir) / tool_prompts_dir) if base_dir else str((config_path.parent / tool_prompts_dir).resolve())
   182→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, 'HARMONIA_TOOL_PROMPTS_DIR', full_tools)
   183→
   184→    # Handle bdikit_models configuration (LLMs used by bdi-kit for schema/value matching)
   185→    bdikit_models = config.get('bdikit_models', {})
   186→    bdikit_model_vars = {
   187→        'instance_matching_llm': 'HARMONIA_LLM_FOR_INSTANCE_MATCHING',
   188→        'numeric_instance_matching_llm': 'HARMONIA_LLM_FOR_NUMERIC_INSTANCE_MATCHING',
   189→        'embedding_model_for_instance_matching': 'HARMONIA_EMBEDDING_MODEL_FOR_INSTANCE_MATCHING',
   190→        'schema_matching_llm': 'HARMONIA_LLM_FOR_SCHEMA_MATCHING',
   191→        'magneto_zero_shot_schema_matching_llm': 'HARMONIA_LLM_FOR_MAGNETO_ZERO_SHOT_SCHEMA_MATCHING',
   192→        'magneto_fine_tuned_schema_matching_llm': 'HARMONIA_LLM_FOR_MAGNETO_FINE_TUNED_SCHEMA_MATCHING',
   193→    }
   194→    for yaml_key, env_var in bdikit_model_vars.items():
   195→        value = bdikit_models.get(yaml_key)
   196→        if value:
   197→            env_content = update_env_value(env_content, env_var, value)
   198→
   199→    # Determine output path
   200→    if output_dir is None:
   201→        output_dir = config_path.parent
   202→
   203→    # Generate output filename: config_name_associated.env
   204→    config_name = config_path.stem  # filename without extension
   205→    output_path = output_dir / f"{config_name}_associated.env"
   206→
   207→    # Write the generated .env file
   208→    output_path.write_text(env_content)
   209→
   210→    return output_path
   211→
   212→
   213→def main():
   214→    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
   215→        description="Generate .env files from experiment configuration YAML files"
   216→    )
   217→    parser.add_argument(
   218→        '--config', '-c',
   219→        type=Path,

   224→        type=Path,

   243→
   244→    configs_to_process = []

   246→    if args.config:

   250→        configs_to_process.append(args.config)

   256→        configs_to_process.extend(args.config_dir.glob('*.yaml'))
   257→        configs_to_process.extend(args.config_dir.glob('*.yml'))
   258→
   259→    if not configs_to_process:

   261→        return 1
   262→
   263→    print(f"Generating .env files from {len(configs_to_process)} config(s)...")
   264→    print(f"Base .env: {args.base_env}")
   265→
   266→    for config_path in configs_to_process:

   273→            print(f"  ✓ {config_path.name} -> {output_path.name}")
   274→        except Exception as e:

   276→
   277→    print("\nDone!")

   279→
   280→
   281→if __name__ == '__main__':

     5→from dataclasses import dataclass, field
     6→from pathlib import Path
     7→from typing import Any, Optional

     9→
    10→
    11→@dataclass
    12→class LLMConfig:

    34→

   345→    async def _receive_until_complete(
   346→        self, parent_msg_id: str, timeout: float
   347→    ) -> AsyncIterator[dict]:
   348→        """Receive messages until the request is complete."""
   349→        end_time = asyncio.get_event_loop().time() + timeout
   350→
   351→        while True:
   352→            remaining = end_time - asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
   353→            if remaining <= 0:
   354→                raise asyncio.TimeoutError()
   355→
   356→            try:
   357→                msg = await asyncio.wait_for(
   358→                    self.ws.receive_json(),
   359→                    timeout=min(remaining, 30.0),
   360→                )
   361→            except asyncio.TimeoutError:
   362→                # Check if we should continue waiting
   363→                if asyncio.get_event_loop().time() < end_time:
   364→                    continue
   365→                raise
   366→
   367→            # Check if this message is for our request
   368→            parent_header = msg.get("parent_header", {})
   369→            if parent_header.get("msg_id") != parent_msg_id:
   370→                continue
   371→
   372→            msg_type = msg.get("msg_type", "")
   373→            yield msg
   374→
   375→            # Check for completion signals
   376→            if msg_type in ("llm_response", "error", "execute_reply"):
   377→                # Final response received
   378→                break
   379→            elif msg_type == "status":
   380→                # Check if kernel is idle (request complete)
   381→                if msg.get("content", {}).get("execution_state") == "idle":
   382→                    break

## Current Model Capabilities

Google's Gemini platform offers context windows ranging from 128,000 to two million tokens depending on model and tier. Gemini 1.5 Pro remains available with an upgradeable window reaching two million tokens—the largest supported by any mainstream model as of late 2025/2026.

## Core Optimization Strategy

The primary optimization when working with long context and the Gemini models is to use context caching. Context caching has been launched in the Gemini API for both Gemini 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash.

## Key Strategic Recommendations

Google's documentation suggests several practical strategies:

1. **Document Organization**: Chunk multi-document uploads and large datasets into logical, referenced sections, using context caching for static information to minimize repeated input.

2. **Structured Prompting**: Use structured prompts that reference specific cached blocks or file segments by unique ID rather than uploading everything in every turn.

3. **Token Monitoring**: Monitor token counters in AI Studio or API dashboards, and plan to summarize or archive older content as the context window fills.

4. **Testing & Scaling**: Test model recall on medium-length segments (100,000–200,000 tokens) before scaling up to the full-million-token workflows to prevent silent truncation or memory loss.

The official Google AI documentation and Vertex AI resources provide detailed guidance on implementing these strategies effectively.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about OpenRouter's middle-out transform context management:

## Overview

The middle-out transform compresses content by removing or truncating content from the middle of the prompt. This helps users extend conversations in part because LLMs pay significantly less attention to the middle of sequences anyway.

## How It Works

When middle-out compression is enabled, OpenRouter will first try to find models whose context length is at least half of your total required tokens. For example, if your prompt requires 10,000 tokens total, models with at least 5,000 context length will be considered. If no models meet this criteria, OpenRouter will fall back to using the model with the highest available context length.

## Message Management

Anthropic's Claude models enforce a maximum of 1000 messages. When this limit is exceeded with middle-out enabled, the transform will keep half of the messages from the start and half from the end of the conversation.

## Default Behavior

All OpenRouter endpoints with 8k (8,192 tokens) or less context length will default to using middle-out. To disable this, set transforms: [] in the request body.

## Documentation

The official OpenRouter documentation on message transforms can be found at https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/message-transforms

## Key Research Areas and Papers

**Agent Context Optimization:**
ACON (Agent Context Optimization) is a framework for compressing both environment observations and interaction histories, tailored to multi-step agent tasks. ACON was validated on three multi-step agent benchmarks (AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Multi-objective QA), demonstrating the ability to lower memory usage by 26–54% while largely maintaining task performance.

**Context Compression Approaches:**
Prior works on context compression can be broadly grouped into three directions: document- or retrieval-based compression, dialogue memory summarization, and low-level KV cache compression.

**Conversation Memory for LLMs:**
Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive conversational abilities, but their fixed context windows severely limit long-term coherence, and even long-context variants can experience performance degradation. One approach represents conversational history as event-like propositions that bundle together participants, temporal cues, and minimal local context.

**Recent Innovations:**
Researchers at Seoul National University developed KVzip, an AI technology that intelligently compresses the conversation memory of LLM-based chatbots used in long-context tasks. Adaptive Focus Memory (AFM) allocates each past message to one of three fidelity levels (FULL, COMPRESSED, or PLACEHOLDER) to preserve salient information while minimizing prompt length.

**Multi-Agent Systems:**
Multi-agent architectures often adopt iterative summarization, such as in MedAgents where a report-assistant agent compresses multi-agent conversations into persistent context for the next round.

## LLMLingua and Related Work (2024)

There are several key papers in the LLMLingua series from 2023-2024:

### LLMLingua (2023)
LLMLingua is a coarse-to-fine prompt compression method that involves a budget controller to maintain semantic integrity under high compression ratios, a token-level iterative compression algorithm to better model the interdependence between compressed contents, and an instruction tuning based method for distribution alignment between language models. The approach yields state-of-the-art performance and allows for up to 20x compression with little performance loss.

### LongLLMLingua (2024)
LongLLMLingua addresses three main challenges in long context scenarios: higher computational cost, performance reduction, and position bias. It uses prompt compression to improve LLMs' perception of key information. In the NaturalQuestions benchmark, LongLLMLingua boosts performance by up to 21.4% with around 4x fewer tokens in GPT-3.5-Turbo, and achieves a 94.0% cost reduction in the LooGLE benchmark.

### LLMLingua-2 (2024)
LLMLingua-2 is a small-size yet powerful prompt compression method trained via data distillation from GPT-4 for token classification with a BERT-level encoder, excels in task-agnostic compression and surpasses LLMLingua in handling out-of-domain data, offering 3x-6x faster performance.

The papers have been published at major conferences including EMNLP 2023 and ACL 2024, with code available on GitHub at microsoft/LLMLingua.

## Key Papers Found:

**1. Sliding Window Attention Training (SWAT) - 2025**
SWAT enables efficient long-context handling via Sliding Window Attention Training, replacing softmax with the sigmoid function and utilizing a balanced ALiBi and Rotary Position Embedding for efficient information compression and retention. SWAT achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with linear recurrent architectures on eight benchmarks. (arXiv:2502.18845, February 2025)

**2. Training-Free Exponential Extension of Sliding Window Context with Cascading KV Cache - 2024**
This proposes a novel mechanism for storing longer sliding window contexts by keeping separate cascading sub-cache buffers whereby each subsequent buffer conditionally accepts a fraction of the relatively more important tokens evicted from the previous buffer. The method shows improvements of 5.6% on long context generation (LongBench), 1.2% in streaming perplexity (PG19), and 0.6% in language understanding (MMLU STEM). (arXiv:2406.17808, June 2024)

**3. Sliding Windows Are Not the End - 2024**
This paper explores the limitations of sliding window approaches for ranking tasks in long-context LLMs. (arXiv:2412.14574, December 2024)

**4. SWAA: Sliding Window Attention Adaptation - 2025**
A more recent work on adaptive sliding window attention strategies for efficient long-context processing. (arXiv:2512.10411, 2025)

## Search Results Summary

I found comprehensive information about the MemGPT paper and its connection to the Letta framework. Here are the key findings:

### Paper Details
The paper is titled "MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems" and has the arXiv identifier 2310.08560. The paper was published in 2023 by Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, Vivian Fang, Shishir G. Patil, and Joseph E. Gonzalez.

### Core Concept
The paper proposes virtual context management, a technique drawing inspiration from hierarchical memory systems in traditional operating systems that provide the appearance of large memory resources through data movement between fast and slow memory, and introduces MemGPT (Memory-GPT), a system that intelligently manages different memory tiers to effectively provide extended context within the LLM's limited context window.

### Applications
The system is evaluated in two domains: document analysis, where MemGPT can analyze large documents that far exceed the underlying LLM's context window, and multi-session chat, where MemGPT can create conversational agents that remember, reflect, and evolve dynamically through long-term interactions with their users.

### Connection to Letta
As of September 2024, MemGPT is part of Letta, an open-source agent framework that helps developers build persistent agents, while MemGPT refers to the agent design pattern with two tiers of memory introduced in the research paper.

You can access the paper directly at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560

Based on the search results, here's what I found about **LangChain ConversationSummaryBufferMemory context management**:

## Overview

ConversationSummaryBufferMemory is a buffer with summarizer for storing conversation memory that provides a running summary of the conversation together with the most recent messages in the conversation under the constraint that the total number of tokens in the conversation does not exceed a certain limit.

## How It Works

The ConversationSummaryBufferMemory is a mix of the ConversationSummaryMemory and the ConversationBufferWindowMemory, as it summarizes the earliest interactions in a conversation while maintaining the max_token_limit most recent tokens in their conversation.

## Key Features

Key parameters include llm (required), max_token_limit (default 2000), memory_key (default 'history'), ai_prefix (default 'AI'), and human_prefix (default 'Human').

The memory provides several important methods:
- Save context from this conversation to buffer
- Prune buffer if it exceeds max token limit
- Predict a new summary based on the messages and existing summary

## Token Management

Despite including a summary of past interactions and the raw form of recent interactions, the increase in token count of ConversationSummaryBufferMemory is competitive with other methods.

## Deprecation Note

ConversationSummaryBufferMemory has been deprecated since version 0.3.1 with a migration guide available, and it will not be removed until langchain==1.0.0.

I've found comprehensive documentation on LlamaIndex's context management, conversation memory, and chat engine features. Here are the key findings:

## Chat Engine Overview

Chat engine is a high-level interface for having a conversation with your data (multiple back-and-forth instead of a single question & answer), similar to ChatGPT but augmented with your knowledge base. It is conceptually a stateful analogy of a Query Engine.

## Context Mode Chat Engine

The Context Chat Engine uses a retriever to retrieve a context, set the context in the system prompt, and then uses an LLM to generate a response, for a fluid chat experience.

### Configuration Example

You can configure the chat engine with `ChatMemoryBuffer.from_defaults(token_limit=1500)` to manage chat history context limits.

## Memory Management

LlamaIndex offers several memory types:

- ChatMemoryBuffer: A basic memory buffer that stores the last X messages that fit into a token limit.
- ChatSummaryMemoryBuffer: A memory buffer that stores the last X messages that fit into a token limit, and also summarizes the conversation periodically when it gets too long.
- VectorMemory: A memory that stores and retrieves chat messages from a vector database. It makes no guarantees about the order of the messages, and returns the most similar messages to the latest user message.

## Chat Stores

Chat history is unique compared to other storage formats, since the order of messages is important for maintaining an overall conversation. Chat stores can organize sequences of chat messages by keys (like user_ids or other unique identifiable strings), and handle delete, insert, and get operations.

The official documentation provides practical examples and detailed implementation guides for all these features.

Based on the web search results, here's comprehensive information about the Ollama `num_ctx` parameter:

## num_ctx Parameter Overview

By default, Ollama uses a context window size of 4096 tokens (though some sources reference older defaults of 2048 tokens). The num_ctx parameter is crucial for adjusting the context length, and when you set it, you essentially tell the model how large of a prompt it should consider when generating its responses.

## Context Length Definition

The context length refers to the maximum number of tokens the model can consider at once when generating responses, and it includes both input tokens (prompt) and output tokens (response).

## Truncation Behavior

A key finding regarding truncation: When Ollama will truncate the prompt so that it fits the num_ctx value, it will trim the prompt from the start, meaning that if the prompt starts with a question, that question will never be sent to the model. Additionally, Ollama silently discards the leading context, which means users may not be aware that data exceeding the context limit has been dropped.

## How to Set num_ctx

When using ollama run, you can use /set parameter num_ctx 4096, and when using the API, you can specify the num_ctx parameter. You can set the num_ctx parameter when launching or running a model by adding /set parameter num_ctx in the CLI, setting OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH as an environment variable, adjusting context size in the Ollama GUI, or passing it in the API options.

## Performance Considerations

Larger num_ctx increases VRAM/RAM usage massively and increases inference time, and increasing context length beyond the training maximum can degrade output quality.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Ollama `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX` environment variable and the runner.go truncation warning:

## The Truncation Warning

There's a warning in the server's logs: `time=2024-12-14T18:01:09.338Z level=WARN source=runner.go:129 msg="truncating input prompt"` which indicates that Ollama is truncating prompts that exceed the context limit. The warning message shows parameters like `limit`, `prompt`, `keep`, and `new` which indicate the context window size and how the prompt is being truncated.

## About OLLAMA_NUM_CTX and Context Windows

You can set the context window size through the environment variable `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH` if you start Ollama from the command line. Note that the environment variable is `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH`, not `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX` (which is the parameter name used in model configuration files).

## Common Issues

Several issues have been reported with context truncation:

- Ollama's OpenAI-compatible API does not respect the `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX` environment variable, and logs may show truncation warnings like `level=WARN msg="truncating input prompt" limit=4096 prompt=10573 keep=4 new=4096`
- When a prompt exceeds the context window, Ollama will truncate the prompt so that it fits the num_ctx value.
- When a conversation's token count exceeds the model's context length, Ollama silently drops older messages from the front of the conversation, with no indication to users that truncation occurred.

I found several relevant resources about agent frameworks and context management for conversation history. Here's a summary of the search results:

## Microsoft Agent Framework

The Microsoft Agent Framework provides built-in support for managing multi-turn conversations with AI agents, including maintaining context across multiple interactions.

AgentSession is the conversation history container, and it accumulates user and assistant messages across multiple RunAsync or RunStreamingAsync calls. You pass the same session instance to every call in a conversation to maintain context.

The AgentSession type is the abstraction that represents chat history and other state of an agent. AIAgent instances are stateless and the same agent instance can be used with multiple AgentSession instances, with all state preserved in the AgentSession.

## Strands Agent Framework

The Strands agent framework offers conversation management through conversation managers. The apply_management method is called after each event loop cycle completes to manage the conversation history, and it's responsible for applying your management strategy to the messages array.

The SlidingWindowConversationManager maintains a fixed window size and automatically removes messages from the window if the number of messages exceeds the limit. The SummarizingConversationManager implements intelligent conversation context management by summarizing older messages instead of simply discarding them, preserving important information while staying within context limits.

## Context Management Strategies

Strategies for managing long conversations include summarizing periodically after every N turns and replacing history with the summary plus last few turns, or trimming old turns and keeping only the last N message pairs.

## Key Surveys

A comprehensive survey on the memory mechanism of LLM-based agents has been proposed, which systematically reviews previous studies on how to design and evaluate the memory module. This survey is available on ACM Transactions on Information Systems.

A comprehensive survey provides an in-depth examination of LLM-based agents and presents a taxonomy that organizes the field into four fundamental categories: reasoning-enhanced agents, tool-augmented agents, multi-agent systems, and memory-augmented agents. This analysis encompasses over 100 papers spanning the period from 2020 to 2024.

## Recent Memory-Augmented Architecture Papers

LLM agents require memory systems to leverage historical experiences, but current memory systems enable basic storage and retrieval while lacking sophisticated memory organization. A novel agentic memory system (A-MEM) that can dynamically organize memories in an agentic way was proposed, following the basic principles of the Zettelkasten method to create interconnected knowledge networks through dynamic indexing and linking.

## Memory Types and Mechanisms

Memory architecture complexity should scale with the model's capabilities: smaller foundation models benefit most from RAG, while more advanced instruction-tuned models benefit from episodic memory and richer semantic memory structures.

Memory stands out as the key component that transforms the original LLM into a "true agent," enabling the agent to maintain long-term context, accumulate and utilize knowledge over time, and coordinate effectively with external sources.

Based on the web search results, here are some key findings on compressive memory transformer and context compression from arXiv in 2024 and recent years:

## Key Papers and Approaches

**Infini-Attention / Infini-Transformer (2024)**
The Infini-attention incorporates a compressive memory into the vanilla attention mechanism and builds in both masked local attention and long-term linear attention mechanisms in a single Transformer block. This approach demonstrates effectiveness on long-context language modeling benchmarks, 1M sequence length passkey context block retrieval and 500K length book summarization tasks with 1B and 8B LLMs.

**Elastic Memory (2026)**
Elastic Memory is a novel memory architecture grounded in the HiPPO framework for online function approximation. It treats historical sequence as samples from continuous signals, applying optimal online compression to encode them into a fixed-size memory state. Elastic Memory consistently outperformed baselines on long-context (32k+) datasets across three domains. With equal parameters, it beat Memorizing Transformer by 16x memory and outperformed Melodi at all memory sizes, even when Melodi had 30% more parameters.

**Gradual Forgetting (2025)**
This approach uses a bank of unimodal temporal filters to produce a log-compressed memory of the distant past, inspired by cognitive models of human memory that posit a logarithmic encoding of temporal information.

**REFORM**
REFORM divides the input into manageable chunks and iteratively processes them while maintaining a summarized representation of prior chunks, typically by compressing or evicting parts of the Key-Value (KV) cache.

These approaches address the quadratic bottleneck in attention when scaling to long contexts, with recent approaches introducing recurrent memory to extend context beyond the current window.

I found comprehensive information about Anthropic Claude's context windows and API reference documentation. Here's a summary of the key findings:

## Context Window Sizes

The Claude API can ingest 1M tokens when using Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, and Sonnet 4, and 200K+ tokens when using all other models.

## 1M Token Context Window (Beta)

The 1M token context window is currently in beta for organizations in usage tier 4 and organizations with custom rate limits, and is only available for Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, and Sonnet 4.

To enable this feature, include the context-1m-2025-08-07 beta header in your API requests.

## Pricing and Rate Limits

Requests exceeding 200K tokens are automatically charged at premium rates (2x input, 1.5x output pricing). Long context requests have dedicated rate limits.

## Context Window Definition

The "context window" refers to all the text a language model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself. A larger context window allows the model to handle more complex and lengthy prompts, but more context isn't automatically better—as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot.

For complete technical documentation and API reference details, visit the official Anthropic documentation at [platform.claude.com/docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs).

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about OpenAI API context summarization and truncation strategies in conversation management. Here are the key findings:

## Context Summarization with Realtime API

OpenAI's approach includes automatic "context trim" that occurs when the token window becomes very large, compressing older turns into a summary, with the strategy of summarizing older turns into a single assistant message while keeping the last few verbatim turns and continuing.

The Realtime API maintains an open, stateful session, and wraps these components inside a simple ConversationState object to keep logic clean, track history, and manage summarization when context windows fill up.

## Implementation Strategies

The cookbook demonstrates two primary approaches:

1. **Context Trimming**: Context trimming drops older turns while keeping the last N turns, providing zero added latency with no extra model calls to compress history and maintaining fidelity for recent work through keeping latest tool results and parameters verbatim.

2. **Context Summarization**: Context summarization compresses prior messages into structured, shorter summaries injected into conversation history, retaining long-range memory compactly while allowing cost-controlled scale with one concise summary replacing hundreds of turns.

## Conversation State Management

For long-running conversations with the Responses API, you can use the /responses/compact endpoint to shrink the context you send with each turn.

The OpenAI Cookbook provides practical implementations and working examples of these patterns for managing conversation context in production applications.

1→# Implementation Plan: Fix Context Size Issues
     2→
     3→**Date:** 25 February 2026
     4→**Scope:** Two fixes — (1) Ollama num_ctx passthrough, (2) FETCH_STATE_CODE budget caps
     5→**Background:** See `documentation/possible_features/25_02_2026_2238_context_management_Archytas_beaker.md`
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Overview
    10→
    11→Two independent fixes to deploy:
    12→
    13→| Fix | Problem | Effort | Risk |
    14→|-----|---------|--------|------|
    15→| Fix 1: Ollama num_ctx | Silent truncation to 4096 tokens on all /api/chat calls | 1 line | Very low |
    16→| Fix 2: FETCH_STATE_CODE budget | Kernel state serialization can produce ~1M tokens | New Python module | Low-medium |
    17→
    18→---
    19→
    20→## Fix 1: Ollama Context Length Passthrough
    21→
    22→### Problem
    23→
    24→`OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=64000` in `.env` is only used during model pre-load (`/api/generate`). Subsequent `/api/chat` calls from Beaker/Archytas don't pass `num_ctx`, so Ollama defaults to 4096 tokens and silently truncates prompts.
    25→
    26→### Solution
    27→
    28→Export `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX` as a server-level environment variable before starting Ollama. This makes Ollama apply the context length globally to all API calls.
    29→
    30→### Exact Change
    31→
    32→**File:** `exec_apptainer_harmonia.sh`
    33→
    34→**Current code (lines 618–622):**
    35→
    36→```bash
    37→# Export OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH if set (controls Ollama's context window allocation)
    38→if [ -n "$OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH" ]; then
    39→    export OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH
    40→    echo "   OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH: ${OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH}"
    41→fi
    42→```
    43→
    44→**New code (replace the above block):**
    45→
    46→```bash
    47→# Export OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH if set (controls Ollama's context window allocation)
    48→if [ -n "$OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH" ]; then
    49→    export OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH
    50→    # Also set OLLAMA_NUM_CTX so Ollama applies this to ALL /api/chat calls,
    51→    # not just the pre-load /api/generate call. Without this, Ollama defaults
    52→    # to num_ctx=4096 and silently truncates prompts. See issue 3H in
    53→    # types_of_log_and_trace_problems.yaml.
    54→    export OLLAMA_NUM_CTX="${OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH}"
    55→    echo "   OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH: ${OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH}"
    56→    echo "   OLLAMA_NUM_CTX:        ${OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH} (server-level default for /api/chat)"
    57→fi
    58→```
    59→
    60→### Verification
    61→
    62→After applying this fix, run an experiment with a local Ollama model and check the Ollama log file for the absence of `truncating input prompt` warnings. Previously, these appeared on virtually every multi-turn experiment.
    63→
    64→```bash
    65→grep "truncating input prompt" logs/*_ollama.log
    66→```
    67→
    68→If the fix works, there should be zero matches in new runs.
    69→
    70→### Important Note on OLLAMA_NUM_CTX
    71→
    72→Per the Ollama FAQ and GitHub issues, the environment variable name is `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX` (not `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH`). The `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH` variable is a Harmonia-specific convention read by `exec_apptainer_harmonia.sh`. The Ollama server itself reads `OLLAMA_NUM_CTX`.
    73→
    74→**Caveat:** Increasing `num_ctx` increases VRAM usage. For a 30B model with `num_ctx=64000`, expect ~4–8 GB additional VRAM for the KV cache on top of model weights. Ensure GPU nodes have sufficient headroom. If a model already saturates VRAM (like nemotron-3-nano on RTX 6000), setting `num_ctx=64000` may cause OOM or force CPU offloading. Consider making `context_length` model-specific in the experiment config YAMLs rather than using a single large value for all models.
    75→
    76→---
    77→
    78→## Fix 2: FETCH_STATE_CODE Kernel State Budget
    79→
    80→### Problem
    81→
    82→Beaker's `FETCH_STATE_CODE` (in `beaker_kernel/subkernels/python.py` lines 27–124) serializes the entire Python kernel namespace to JSON. When BDI loads the GDC schema vocabulary, this serialized state can balloon to ~1M tokens, exceeding any model's context window. The existing truncation (99 items for lists, `.head()` for DataFrames) is insufficient because the GDC schema is deeply nested dicts, not flat lists.
    83→
    84→### Solution
    85→
    86→Create a new Python module `src/context_management/kernel_state_budget.py` that post-processes the FETCH_STATE_CODE output before it reaches Beaker's auto-context formatting. This module implements three configurable strategies:
    87→
    88→1. **Per-variable size cap**: Drop any single variable whose JSON exceeds a threshold (default: 20K chars). Replace with a placeholder.
    89→2. **Total budget cap**: If the total serialized state exceeds a budget (default: 50K chars), stop adding variables and append a truncation warning.
    90→3. **Type blacklist**: Exclude variables of certain types entirely (e.g., BDI internal objects).
    91→
    92→### Architecture
    93→
    94→```
    95→[FETCH_STATE_CODE output]  (original, potentially huge)
    96→         │
    97→         ▼
    98→[kernel_state_budget.py::apply_budget()]
    99→         │
   100→         ├─ Step 1: Remove blacklisted types
   101→         ├─ Step 2: Remove oversized individual variables
   102→         ├─ Step 3: Enforce total budget (drop remaining large vars)
   103→         │
   104→         ▼
   105→[Budgeted state JSON]  (guaranteed ≤ total_budget chars)
   106→         │
   107→         ▼
   108→[Beaker auto_context()]  (formats as Markdown + JSON)
   109→```
   110→
   111→### Integration Point
   112→
   113→The budget enforcement is applied by monkey-patching Beaker's `get_subkernel_state()` method at experiment startup. This avoids modifying the installed `.venv` packages.
   114→
   115→**File:** `src/context_management/__init__.py`
   116→
   117→```python
   118→"""Context management utilities for controlling kernel state size in Beaker/Archytas."""
   119→```
   120→
   121→**File:** `src/context_management/kernel_state_budget.py`
   122→
   123→```python
   124→"""
   125→Kernel State Budget Enforcement
   126→
   127→Post-processes FETCH_STATE_CODE output to prevent context window explosions.
   128→Three configurable strategies:
   129→  1. Per-variable size cap (default: 20K chars)
   130→  2. Total budget cap (default: 50K chars)
   131→  3. Type blacklist (default: common BDI internal types)
   132→
   133→Usage:
   134→    from src.context_management.kernel_state_budget import apply_budget
   135→
   136→    # Apply with defaults
   137→    budgeted_state = apply_budget(raw_state)
   138→
   139→    # Apply with custom config
   140→    budgeted_state = apply_budget(raw_state, config=BudgetConfig(
   141→        max_variable_size=10_000,
   142→        total_budget=30_000,
   143→        type_blacklist=["SchemaGraph", "SimilarityFloodingMatcher"],
   144→    ))
   145→"""
   146→
   147→import json
   148→import logging
   149→from dataclasses import dataclass, field
   150→
   151→logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
   152→
   153→# Default type blacklist: BDI/schema types known to produce huge serializations
   154→DEFAULT_TYPE_BLACKLIST = [
   155→    "SchemaGraph",
   156→    "SimilarityFloodingMatcher",
   157→    "ColumnMappingSpec",
   158→    "ValueMappingSpec",
   159→]
   160→
   161→
   162→@dataclass
   163→class BudgetConfig:
   164→    """Configuration for kernel state budget enforcement."""
   165→
   166→    # Maximum JSON size (in characters) for any single variable.
   167→    # Variables exceeding this are replaced with a placeholder.
   168→    # Set to 0 to disable per-variable limiting.
   169→    max_variable_size: int = 20_000
   170→
   171→    # Maximum total JSON size (in characters) for the entire state.
   172→    # Once this budget is reached, remaining variables are dropped.
   173→    # Set to 0 to disable total budget limiting.
   174→    total_budget: int = 50_000
   175→
   176→    # List of type name substrings to exclude entirely.
   177→    # If a variable's "type" field contains any of these strings, it is dropped.
   178→    # Case-sensitive. Matches anywhere in the type string.
   179→    type_blacklist: list[str] = field(default_factory=lambda: list(DEFAULT_TYPE_BLACKLIST))
   180→
   181→    # Whether to add a "_budget_metadata" key to the output showing what was dropped.
   182→    include_metadata: bool = True
   183→
   184→
   185→def _measure_json_size(obj: object) -> int:
   186→    """Measure the JSON serialization size of an object in characters."""
   187→    try:
   188→        return len(json.dumps(obj, default=str))
   189→    except (TypeError, ValueError, OverflowError):
   190→        return 0
   191→
   192→
   193→def _make_placeholder(var_name: str, var_info: dict, json_size: int, reason: str) -> dict:
   194→    """Create a placeholder dict for a dropped variable."""
   195→    var_type = var_info.get("type", "unknown")
   196→    return {
   197→        "type": var_type,
   198→        "value": f"<dropped: {reason}, original_size={json_size:,} chars, type={var_type}>",
   199→        "_dropped": True,
   200→        "_reason": reason,
   201→        "_original_size": json_size,
   202→    }
   203→
   204→
   205→def apply_budget(raw_state: dict, config: BudgetConfig | None = None) -> dict:
   206→    """
   207→    Apply budget constraints to FETCH_STATE_CODE output.
   208→
   209→    Args:
   210→        raw_state: The raw dictionary returned by FETCH_STATE_CODE, with keys
   211→                   "modules", "variables", "functions", "classes".
   212→        config: Budget configuration. Uses defaults if None.
   213→
   214→    Returns:
   215→        A new dictionary with the same structure but large/blacklisted variables
   216→        replaced with placeholders or removed.
   217→    """
   218→    if config is None:
   219→        config = BudgetConfig()
   220→
   221→    if not raw_state or not isinstance(raw_state, dict):
   222→        return raw_state
   223→

   225→        "modules": raw_state.get("modules", {}),
   226→        "functions": raw_state.get("functions", {}),
   227→        "classes": raw_state.get("classes", {}),
   228→    }
   229→
   230→    variables = raw_state.get("variables", {})
   231→    budgeted_variables = {}
   232→
   233→    # Tracking metadata
   234→    dropped_blacklist = []
   235→    dropped_oversized = []
   236→    dropped_budget_exceeded = []
   237→    total_original_size = 0
   238→    running_total = _measure_json_size(result)  # Start with non-variable overhead
   239→    budget_exceeded = False
   240→
   241→    # Pre-compute sizes for all variables
   242→    var_sizes = {}
   243→    for var_name, var_info in variables.items():
   244→        size = _measure_json_size(var_info)
   245→        var_sizes[var_name] = size
   246→        total_original_size += size
   247→
   248→    # Sort variables by size ascending so we fit as many as possible within budget
   249→    sorted_vars = sorted(variables.items(), key=lambda kv: var_sizes[kv[0]])
   250→
   251→    for var_name, var_info in sorted_vars:
   252→        var_size = var_sizes[var_name]
   253→
   254→        # Step 1: Check type blacklist
   255→        var_type = str(var_info.get("type", ""))
   256→        if config.type_blacklist and any(bl in var_type for bl in config.type_blacklist):
   257→            placeholder = _make_placeholder(var_name, var_info, var_size, "blacklisted_type")

   259→            running_total += _measure_json_size(placeholder)

   261→            logger.info(

   263→                f"size={var_size:,}) — blacklisted type"

   271→                f"exceeds_max_variable_size({config.max_variable_size:,})"

   278→                f"size={var_size:,}) — exceeds max_variable_size={config.max_variable_size:,}"

   298→
   299→        # Variable passes all checks — include as-is
   300→        budgeted_variables[var_name] = var_info
   301→        running_total += var_size
   302→
   303→    result["variables"] = budgeted_variables
   304→
   305→    # Add metadata if configured
   306→    if config.include_metadata:
   307→        total_dropped = len(dropped_blacklist) + len(dropped_oversized) + len(dropped_budget_exceeded)
   308→        if total_dropped > 0:
   309→            result["_budget_metadata"] = {
   310→                "budget_applied": True,
   311→                "config": {
   312→                    "max_variable_size": config.max_variable_size,
   313→                    "total_budget": config.total_budget,
   314→                    "type_blacklist": config.type_blacklist,
   315→                },
   316→                "original_variables_size_chars": total_original_size,
   317→                "final_state_size_chars": running_total,
   318→                "compression_ratio": (
   319→                    round(total_original_size / max(running_total, 1), 1)
   320→                    if total_original_size > 0 else 1.0
   321→                ),
   322→                "dropped_count": total_dropped,
   323→                "dropped_blacklisted": len(dropped_blacklist),
   324→                "dropped_oversized": len(dropped_oversized),
   325→                "dropped_budget_exceeded": len(dropped_budget_exceeded),
   326→                "dropped_details": (
   327→                    dropped_blacklist + dropped_oversized + dropped_budget_exceeded
   328→                ),
   329→            }
   330→        else:
   331→            result["_budget_metadata"] = {
   332→                "budget_applied": True,
   333→                "original_variables_size_chars": total_original_size,
   334→                "final_state_size_chars": running_total,
   335→                "dropped_count": 0,
   336→            }
   337→
   338→    return result

   341→### Integration: Monkey-Patching Beaker's get_subkernel_state
   342→
   343→**File:** `src/context_management/patch_beaker.py`
   344→
   345→```python
   346→"""
   347→Monkey-patch Beaker's get_subkernel_state() to apply kernel state budget.
   348→
   349→Call patch_beaker_state_budget() once at experiment startup, AFTER Beaker's
   350→context has been initialized. This wraps the original method so that the
   351→FETCH_STATE_CODE output is post-processed through apply_budget() before
   352→being formatted as auto-context.
   353→
   354→Usage in run_experiment.py or exec_apptainer_harmonia.sh startup:
   355→
   356→    from src.context_management.patch_beaker import patch_beaker_state_budget
   357→    from src.context_management.kernel_state_budget import BudgetConfig
   358→
   359→    # With defaults (20K per var, 50K total)
   360→    patch_beaker_state_budget(beaker_context)
   361→
   362→    # With custom config
   363→    patch_beaker_state_budget(beaker_context, config=BudgetConfig(
   364→        max_variable_size=30_000,
   365→        total_budget=80_000,
   366→    ))
   367→"""
   368→
   369→import functools
   370→import logging
   371→
   372→from src.context_management.kernel_state_budget import BudgetConfig, apply_budget
   373→
   374→logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
   375→
   376→
   377→def patch_beaker_state_budget(
   378→    beaker_context,
   379→    config: BudgetConfig | None = None,
   380→) -> None:
   381→    """
   382→    Monkey-patch a BeakerContext instance's get_subkernel_state() to apply budget.
   383→
   384→    Args:
   385→        beaker_context: The BeakerContext instance (from beaker_kernel.lib.context).
   386→        config: Budget configuration. Uses defaults if None.
   387→    """
   388→    if config is None:
   389→        config = BudgetConfig()
   390→
   391→    original_method = beaker_context.get_subkernel_state
   392→
   393→    @functools.wraps(original_method)
   394→    async def patched_get_subkernel_state():
   395→        raw_state = await original_method()
   396→        if raw_state:
   397→            budgeted = apply_budget(raw_state, config=config)
   398→            meta = budgeted.get("_budget_metadata", {})
   399→            if meta.get("dropped_count", 0) > 0:
   400→                logger.warning(
   401→                    f"Kernel state budget enforced: dropped {meta['dropped_count']} variables, "
   402→                    f"compressed {meta.get('original_variables_size_chars', 0):,} → "
   403→                    f"{meta.get('final_state_size_chars', 0):,} chars "
   404→                    f"({meta.get('compression_ratio', 1)}x)"
   405→                )
   406→            return budgeted
   407→        return raw_state
   408→
   409→    beaker_context.get_subkernel_state = patched_get_subkernel_state
   410→    logger.info(
   411→        f"Beaker state budget patch applied: max_variable_size={config.max_variable_size:,}, "
   412→        f"total_budget={config.total_budget:,}, "
   413→        f"type_blacklist={config.type_blacklist}"
   414→    )
   415→```

   417→### Integration into run_experiment.py
   418→
   419→The patch needs to be applied after the BeakerClient connects but before the experiment turns begin. However, since `run_experiment.py` communicates with Beaker over WebSocket (it doesn't have direct access to the `BeakerContext` object — that lives inside the Apptainer container), the monkey-patch approach must be applied **inside the container**.
   420→
   421→There are two viable integration approaches:
   422→
   423→#### Approach A: Beaker startup hook (Preferred)
   424→
   425→Add a Beaker context startup hook that applies the patch. This requires modifying the context configuration.
   426→
   427→**File to modify:** The Beaker context's `setup()` method or the context YAML configuration.
   428→
   429→Look at how the Beaker context is initialized inside the container. The `bdikit_context` or `codeact_context` likely has a setup phase where the patch can be applied. Specifically:
   430→
   431→1. Find the context file used by the experiment (check `config.context` in the YAML, e.g., `codeact_context` or `bdikit_context`)
   432→2. Locate the context's Python module inside the container (likely under `/jupyter/src/` or similar)
   433→3. Add the patch call in the context's `setup()` or `__init__()` method
   434→
   435→#### Approach B: Custom FETCH_STATE_CODE override
   436→
   437→Instead of monkey-patching, override `FETCH_STATE_CODE` directly by embedding the budget logic as inline Python code that runs inside the kernel. This avoids the integration complexity of approach A.
   438→
   439→**File to modify:** `.venv/lib/python3.11/site-packages/beaker_kernel/subkernels/python.py`
   440→
   441→Add budget enforcement at the end of `FETCH_STATE_CODE` (before the final `json.dumps`), making it self-contained. The budget parameters would be embedded as constants in the code string.
   442→
   443→**This is the simpler approach** but requires modifying the installed package (fragile across reinstalls). To make it durable, also add a verification step to the Apptainer build that checks the patch is in place.
   444→
   445→#### Approach C: Standalone post-processing in run_experiment.py (Alternative)
   446→
   447→If neither A nor B is feasible, intercept the WebSocket messages in `run_experiment.py` and post-process the kernel state before it's sent to the LLM. This would require:
   448→
   449→1. Parsing incoming WebSocket messages from Beaker
   450→2. Identifying messages that contain kernel state
   451→3. Applying `apply_budget()` to the state
   452→4. Forwarding the budgeted state
   453→
   454→This is more complex and fragile. Only use if A and B are not viable.
   455→
   456→### Recommended Integration: Approach B (Inline in FETCH_STATE_CODE)
   457→
   458→Since the Beaker context runs inside an Apptainer container, and `run_experiment.py` communicates over WebSocket, the cleanest approach is to embed the budget logic directly into `FETCH_STATE_CODE`. This makes the budget enforcement happen at the source — inside the kernel — before the state ever leaves the Jupyter process.
   459→
   460→**Implementation steps:**
   461→
   462→1. Create `src/context_management/kernel_state_budget.py` as the canonical Python module (for testing, documentation, and potential future use outside FETCH_STATE_CODE).
   463→
   464→2. Create `src/context_management/fetch_state_code_patch.py` that generates a modified `FETCH_STATE_CODE` string with budget enforcement embedded:
   465→
   466→```python
   467→"""
   468→Generate a patched FETCH_STATE_CODE string with inline budget enforcement.
   469→
   470→The generated code string is self-contained — it requires no imports and runs
   471→inside the Beaker Jupyter kernel. Budget parameters are baked into the code
   472→as constants.
   473→"""
   474→
   475→
   476→def generate_patched_fetch_state_code(
   477→    max_variable_size: int = 20_000,
   478→    total_budget: int = 50_000,
   479→    type_blacklist: list[str] | None = None,
   480→) -> str:
   481→    """
   482→    Generate a FETCH_STATE_CODE string with budget enforcement.
   483→
   484→    The returned string includes the original FETCH_STATE_CODE logic PLUS
   485→    a post-processing step that applies budget constraints to _result
   486→    before returning it.
   487→
   488→    Args:
   489→        max_variable_size: Max JSON chars per variable (0 to disable).
   490→        total_budget: Max total JSON chars for entire state (0 to disable).
   491→        type_blacklist: Type name substrings to exclude.
   492→
   493→    Returns:
   494→        A Python code string suitable for assigning to
   495→        beaker_kernel.subkernels.python.PythonSubkernel.FETCH_STATE_CODE
   496→    """
   497→    if type_blacklist is None:
   498→        type_blacklist = [
   499→            "SchemaGraph",
   500→            "SimilarityFloodingMatcher",
   501→            "ColumnMappingSpec",
   502→            "ValueMappingSpec",
   503→        ]
   504→
   505→    blacklist_repr = repr(type_blacklist)
   506→
   507→    # This is the BUDGET ENFORCEMENT code appended to the end of the original
   508→    # FETCH_STATE_CODE, just before the final json.dumps return.
   509→    # It operates on `_result` which is the dict built by the original code.
   510→    budget_code = f"""
   511→# === BUDGET ENFORCEMENT (added by Harmonia context_management) ===
   512→import json as _budget_json
   513→
   514→_BUDGET_MAX_VAR_SIZE = {max_variable_size}
   515→_BUDGET_TOTAL = {total_budget}
   516→_BUDGET_TYPE_BLACKLIST = {blacklist_repr}
   517→
   518→def _apply_state_budget(_state):
   519→    if not _state or not isinstance(_state, dict):
   520→        return _state
   521→    _vars = _state.get("variables", {{}})
   522→    _budgeted = {{}}
   523→    _running = 0
   524→    _dropped = 0
   525→
   526→    # Sort by size ascending to fit as many as possible
   527→    _sized = []
   528→    for _vn, _vi in _vars.items():
   529→        try:
   530→            _vs = len(_budget_json.dumps(_vi, default=str))
   531→        except Exception:
   532→            _vs = 0
   533→        _sized.append((_vn, _vi, _vs))
   534→    _sized.sort(key=lambda x: x[2])
   535→
   536→    for _vn, _vi, _vs in _sized:
   537→        _vt = str(_vi.get("type", ""))
   538→
   539→        # Blacklist check
   540→        if any(_bl in _vt for _bl in _BUDGET_TYPE_BLACKLIST):
   541→            _budgeted[_vn] = {{"type": _vt, "value": f"<dropped: blacklisted_type, size={{_vs:,}}>", "_dropped": True}}
   542→            _dropped += 1
   543→            continue
   544→
   545→        # Per-variable size check
   546→        if _BUDGET_MAX_VAR_SIZE > 0 and _vs > _BUDGET_MAX_VAR_SIZE:
   547→            _budgeted[_vn] = {{"type": _vt, "value": f"<dropped: size={{_vs:,}} > max={{_BUDGET_MAX_VAR_SIZE:,}}>", "_dropped": True}}
   548→            _dropped += 1
   549→            continue
   550→
   551→        # Total budget check
   552→        if _BUDGET_TOTAL > 0 and (_running + _vs) > _BUDGET_TOTAL:
   553→            _budgeted[_vn] = {{"type": _vt, "value": f"<dropped: total_budget_exceeded, size={{_vs:,}}>", "_dropped": True}}
   554→            _dropped += 1
   555→            continue
   556→
   557→        _budgeted[_vn] = _vi
   558→        _running += _vs
   559→
   560→    _state["variables"] = _budgeted
   561→    if _dropped > 0:
   562→        _state["_budget_metadata"] = {{"dropped_count": _dropped, "budget_total": _BUDGET_TOTAL, "max_var_size": _BUDGET_MAX_VAR_SIZE}}
   563→    return _state
   564→
   565→_result = _apply_state_budget(_result)
   566→# === END BUDGET ENFORCEMENT ===
   567→"""
   568→    return budget_code
   569→```
   570→
   571→3. Apply the patch at Apptainer container startup or in `exec_apptainer_harmonia.sh` by modifying the Beaker subkernel's `FETCH_STATE_CODE` attribute. This can be done via a Python one-liner executed inside the container:
   572→
   573→```python
   574→# In the Beaker context setup or via a startup script:
   575→from beaker_kernel.subkernels.python import PythonSubkernel
   576→from src.context_management.fetch_state_code_patch import generate_patched_fetch_state_code
   577→
   578→# Get original code
   579→original = PythonSubkernel.FETCH_STATE_CODE
   580→# Insert budget enforcement before the final json.dumps return
   581→patch = generate_patched_fetch_state_code(
   582→    max_variable_size=20_000,
   583→    total_budget=50_000,
   584→)
   585→# The budget code operates on _result, so insert it before the final serialization
   586→# Find the last json.dumps call and insert before it
   587→PythonSubkernel.FETCH_STATE_CODE = original.rstrip() + "\n" + patch
   588→```
